message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support stating that. The report explicitly leaves it open: no arm of the trial reorganised work without reducing hours, so the trial can't show whether the hours cut was necessary.

The one piece of evidence you found points, weakly, the other way. Two control offices cut meetings without changing hours and saw a 4.1% rise in output per hour. That's two offices with no comparison group, so it doesn't establish that reorganisation alone works. But it certainly doesn't show that the hours cut is essential.

What you can say:

> Part of the per-hour gain ran through fewer recurring meetings. Whether the hours cut is needed to deliver this, or whether reorganising meetings alone would capture much of it, is untested: no trial has compared the two directly. Two offices that cut meetings without reducing hours saw a smaller per-hour gain (4.1%), but this was unplanned and uncontrolled.

If the board's decision depends on this question, consider proposing a test: run some offices on a meeting audit only, alongside offices with the hours cut, before rolling out more widely.
